samples.text:
The chart gives information about how much money households in one country spend each week on five categories in 1990, 2005 and 2020.

Housing was the biggest spending in all three years. In 1990 it was $95 per week, then it increased to $150 in 2005 and reached to $240 in 2020. Food was the second in 1990 with $80, and it also rise steadily to $95 and then to $110.

Transport and leisure went up as well. Spending on transport was $55 in 1990 but it grew to $85 in 2005 and $105 in 2020, so it almost doubled. Leisure increase from $40 to $70 and then to $90. On the other hand, clothing was different because it was quite stable. It went up a little to $38 in 2005 but after that it dropped to $30, which is the lowest figure in the chart.

Overall, spending on most of categories increased over the period, especially housing, while spending on clothing decreased slightly at the end.
samples.why: Figures accurate and all categories covered · overview only at the end and basic · linking mechanical and repetitive · adequate vocabulary · several tense and word-form errors that do not impede meaning.

samples.text:
The bar chart illustrates the average amount that households in a particular country spent per week on five categories of goods and services in 1990, 2005 and 2020.

Overall, weekly expenditure rose in four of the five categories, with housing showing by far the largest increase and remaining the biggest expense throughout. Clothing was the only category in which spending fell over the period as a whole.

Housing was already the most expensive item in 1990, at $95 a week, and it climbed to $150 in 2005 before reaching $240 in 2020, around two and a half times the original figure. Spending on food grew at a much slower pace, from $80 to $95 and then to $110, so the gap between food and housing widened considerably.

Transport and leisure followed similar upward trends. Weekly transport costs nearly doubled, increasing from $55 to $105, while the amount spent on leisure more than doubled, going from $40 in 1990 to $90 in 2020. In contrast, clothing expenditure remained fairly stable, rising marginally to $38 in 2005 before falling back to $30, making it the smallest category at the end of period.
samples.why: Clear overview of main trends · key changes highlighted with accurate figures · logical progression and varied linking · some less common vocabulary · mostly error-free with one minor article slip.

samples.text:
The chart compares the average weekly sums spent by households in one country on housing, food, transport, leisure and clothing at three points between 1990 and 2020.

The most notable feature is the sharp and sustained rise in housing costs, which were consistently the largest outlay and grew far faster than any other item. Expenditure on food, transport and leisure also increased steadily, whereas clothing was the sole category to decline.

In 1990, households spent $95 a week on housing, only marginally more than the $80 devoted to food. Over the following three decades, however, the two diverged markedly: housing costs rose to $150 in 2005 and $240 in 2020, an increase of $145, while spending on food edged up to just $110. By the end of the period, therefore, households were spending more than twice as much on housing as on food.

Transport and leisure registered comparable growth. Transport spending almost doubled from $55 to $105, bringing it close to the level of food, and leisure spending more than doubled, climbing from $40 to $90. Clothing, by contrast, barely changed, increasing slightly to $38 in 2005 before slipping to $30 in 2020, the lowest figure recorded for any category.
samples.why: Well-selected key features and a clear overview · accurate figures used for meaningful comparison · seamless cohesion · precise, natural vocabulary · wide range of structures with no noticeable errors.
